section.title: Ruth at the Threshing Floor
section.sectionRationale: The third act is the bold night at the threshing floor. Naomi plans a resting place for Ruth, Ruth appeals to Boaz to spread his garment over her as redeemer, and Boaz responds with integrity, promising to settle the matter while honoring a nearer kinsman first. It is one tense, tender movement in which the request for redemption is made and answered in principle.
section.thesis: A vulnerable widow risks everything to appeal to her redeemer for covering and rest, and the worthy Boaz answers her faith not with exploitation but with honor, a pledge, and the promise that he will not rest until redemption is secured.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Naomi's plan for Ruth's rest; the appeal at the threshing floor, spread your garment over me; Boaz's honorable response and pledge; and Ruth's return with the sign of six measures of barley.

units.label: Naomi's plan for Ruth's rest
units.note: should I not seek a resting place for you

verses.text: One day Ruth’s mother-in-law Naomi said to her, “My daughter, should I not seek a {{menuchah|resting place}} for you, that it may be well with you?
Now is not Boaz, with whose servant girls you have been working, a relative of ours? In fact, tonight he is winnowing barley on the threshing floor.
Therefore wash yourself, put on perfume, and wear your best clothes. Go down to the threshing floor, but do not let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, note the place where he lies. Then go in and uncover his feet, and lie down, and he will explain to you what you should do.”
“I will do everything you say,” Ruth answered.
So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had instructed her to do.

units.label: The appeal at the threshing floor
units.note: spread the corner of your garment over me

verses.text: After Boaz had finished eating and drinking and was in good spirits, he went to lie down at the end of the heap of grain. Then Ruth went in secretly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
At midnight, Boaz was startled, turned over, and there lying at his feet was a woman!
“Who are you?” he asked. “I am your servant Ruth,” she replied. “Spread the corner of your {{kanaph|garment}} over me, for you are a {{goel|kinsman-redeemer}}.”
Then Boaz said, “May the LORD bless you, my daughter. You have shown more {{chesed|kindness}} now than before, because you have not run after the younger men, whether rich or poor.
And now do not be afraid, my daughter. I will do for you whatever you request, since all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of {{chayil|noble character}}.
Yes, it is true that I am a kinsman-redeemer, but there is a redeemer nearer than I.
Stay here tonight, and in the morning, if he wants to redeem you, good. Let him redeem you. But if he does not want to redeem you, as surely as the LORD lives, I will. Now lie here until morning.”
So she lay down at his feet until morning, but she got up before anyone else could recognize her. Then Boaz said, “Do not let it be known that a woman came to the threshing floor.”
And he told her, “Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out.” When she did so, he poured in six measures of barley and placed it on her. Then he went into the city.
When Ruth returned to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked her, “How did it go, my daughter?” Then Ruth told her all that Boaz had done for her.
And she said, “He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, ‘Do not go back to your mother-in-law empty-handed.’”
“Wait, my daughter,” said Naomi, “until you find out how things go, for he will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today.”

menuchah.gloss: Rest, a resting place, security, a settled home. Naomi seeks a menuchah for Ruth, the security of marriage and a household after years of vulnerability. The idea of God-given rest runs through Scripture, from the promised land to the deep rest Christ gives to the weary, Matthew 11:28.

kanaph.gloss: Wing, edge, or corner of a garment. Ruth asks Boaz to spread the corner of his garment, his kanaph, over her, a gesture of protection and a proposal of marriage. It deliberately echoes 2:12, where Boaz blessed Ruth for taking refuge under the wings, kanaph, of God; now she asks him to be the very shelter he prayed for.

goel.gloss: Kinsman-redeemer or guardian-redeemer, the near relative legally responsible to rescue his kin, buy back family land, and raise up a name for the dead. The BSB footnote points to Leviticus 25:25-55. Ruth appeals to Boaz precisely as a goel, asking him to take up the redeemer's role for her and Naomi.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast love, loyal kindness beyond duty. Boaz praises Ruth's later kindness, her chesed, in seeking a redeemer for the family's sake rather than chasing younger men. The word ties her act to the book's great theme and to the covenant faithfulness that God Himself shows.

chayil.gloss: Strength, worth, valor, noble character. Boaz calls Ruth an eshet chayil, a woman of noble character, the same phrase used of the excellent woman in Proverbs 31:10 and the counterpart to his own description as a gibbor chayil in 2:1. The whole town knows her worth; a worthy woman meets a worthy man.

basic.context: Naomi wants to secure Ruth's future, so she sends her at night to the threshing floor where Boaz is sleeping after the winnowing. Following Naomi's plan, Ruth lies at his feet and, when he wakes, asks him to spread his garment over her because he is a kinsman-redeemer, in effect a proposal of marriage and a plea for covering. Boaz responds with honor and joy, promises to act, but tells her there is a nearer redeemer who must be given first refusal. He sends her home with grain and a pledge to settle it that very day.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a tense, carefully told scene that modern readers can misread. The language is charged but the narrative goes out of its way to show that both Ruth and Boaz act with integrity. Ruth's request to spread the garment is covenant language for marriage and protection, not seduction. Boaz's care to honor the nearer kinsman shows righteousness, not reluctance.
basic.originalLanguages: Naomi seeks a menuchah, a resting place, for Ruth. Ruth asks Boaz to spread his kanaph, the corner of his garment, over her, the same word for the wings of God under which she took refuge in chapter two. She appeals to him as a goel, a kinsman-redeemer. Boaz praises her chesed, loyal kindness, and calls her an eshet chayil, a woman of noble character.
basic.typology: Boaz spreading his garment over Ruth pictures Christ covering His people, taking them as His own and giving them rest. Ruth's bold approach in humility and faith mirrors the way sinners come to Christ, casting themselves on the mercy and right of a redeemer who is able and willing to save.
basic.christ: Boaz, willing to redeem and covering Ruth with his garment, foreshadows Jesus, who covers our shame with His own righteousness and takes us as His bride. Just as Boaz would not rest until the matter of redemption was settled, Christ did not rest until our redemption was accomplished at the cross.
basic.god: God's providence keeps working through wise plans and faithful people. We learn that God gives rest and security to the vulnerable, that He honors integrity, and that He is drawing the whole situation toward redemption, even though His name is spoken more in blessing than in visible action.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 16 pictures God spreading His garment over His people in covenant love. Proverbs 31 celebrates the woman of noble character Ruth is called. And Christ's covering of His bride appears in Ephesians 5 and Revelation 19.
basic.oneStory: The redemption story tightens as Ruth asks to be covered by her redeemer and Boaz pledges to act. The garment spread over the widow points ahead to Christ covering His people and giving them rest, and Boaz's refusal to rest until it is settled foreshadows the Redeemer who finishes the work of salvation.

context.literary:
Ruth 3 is built as a night mirror to the daylight scene of chapter two. There Ruth gleaned in the open field under the sun and among many eyes; here she comes to the threshing floor after dark and stays hidden until the eyes of Bethlehem are shut. The narrator marks the change of setting by repeating the verb lie down across the space of a few verses, first of Boaz settling for the night, then of Ruth positioning herself at his feet, so that the whole scene turns on a single small, freighted action.

The unit is framed by two speeches of instruction that Ruth carries out to the letter. Naomi's plan in verses 1 to 4 runs through five imperatives, wash, anoint, dress, go down, wait, and verse 6 answers with a flat notice that she did all that her mother in law had instructed, holding the plan and its execution side by side without comment. The same shape returns at the end: Boaz instructs Ruth to bring her shawl and hold it out, and she does exactly that, so the chapter opens and closes on obedience carried out precisely.

A second frame runs through the address my daughter. Naomi uses it to open the chapter, and Boaz uses it twice at its center, in effect stepping into something like the protective role Naomi has held, even as he answers Ruth as a woman he might marry. The scene also answers chapter one's emptiness with a concrete image: Ruth returns carrying grain in her shawl, a small but pointed reversal of the empty hands Naomi described on her own return to Bethlehem.

The chapter's suspense comes from what it withholds. The narrator does not tell readers in advance whether Boaz is the nearer kinsman, so the appearance of an unnamed nearer redeemer in verse 12 creates a genuine complication that only chapter four will resolve, turning what could have been a tidy proposal scene into the story's central unanswered question.
context.historical:
The threshing floor sat on raised, wind exposed ground outside town, and at harvest time it was normal for the owner or his workers to sleep beside the winnowed grain overnight, guarding it from thieves and animals until it could be carried in. Naomi's plan depends on this ordinary custom: a woman could reasonably expect to find Boaz there after the day's winnowing, and could approach him without immediately raising alarm, provided she came and left unseen.

Ruth's washing, anointing, and change of clothes were the preparations of a woman making herself ready to be seen and courted, not merely tidiness; ancient readers would have recognized bridal preparation in the list, much as they would recognize a wedding gift in six measures of barley. The narrator's note that Boaz was in good spirits uses an idiom found elsewhere in scenes of satisfied, wine loosened men at the end of a feast, Nabal in 1 Samuel 25:36 and the guests watching Amnon in 2 Samuel 13:28, both scenes where something dangerous follows a full stomach and an open heart. Here the same kind of idiom sets up a moment of real vulnerability for Boaz, which he meets with restraint rather than advantage.

The barley harvest that frames Ruth 2 and 3 fell in spring, near the season of Passover, when Israel remembered its own rescue from slavery; a story about a poor widow finding a redeemer unfolds against the yearly festival of redemption. Threshing floors elsewhere in Scripture become sites of decision and worship, as when David later buys Araunah's threshing floor for an altar, 2 Samuel 24:18-25, so a Bethlehem threshing floor becoming the place a redeemer is secured fits a wider biblical pattern.
context.canonical:
Naomi's opening wish that Ruth find a resting place directly echoes her own words in Ruth 1:9, where she blessed her daughters in law to find rest in the house of a husband; the plan of chapter three is Naomi finally acting to answer the very blessing she once could only speak. The betrothal scene itself plays against a recognizable Old Testament pattern, a man and woman meeting at a well or a spring, as with Abraham's servant and Rebekah, Genesis 24:10-27, Jacob and Rachel, Genesis 29:1-12, and Moses and Zipporah, Exodus 2:15-21. Ruth's meeting with Boaz departs from that pattern in every particular, no well, no daytime, and it is the woman rather than the man's family who initiates the approach, which sharpens how unusual and risky her faith filled boldness truly was.

The scene also stands beside, without simply repeating, the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25:5-10; the goel of Leviticus 25 and the levir of that law are related but not identical institutions, and Ruth 3 and 4 blend them into a single act of family rescue that neither text alone quite anticipated, showing how Israel's law could be applied with wisdom to a case Scripture had not exactly foreseen. And Boaz's blessing over a woman of noble character sets up Ruth 4's genealogy of a house built like Rachel and Leah, so that this quiet night scene stands in the company of the mothers who built up the house of Israel.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator wants his hearers to see two kinds of courage meeting in the dark: a woman's bold, humble faith and a man's restrained, righteous integrity, and to feel that neither cancels the other out. Ruth's approach is startling by any standard of propriety, yet the author takes pains to show that she asks for exactly what the law and custom allow her to ask, marriage and redemption, nothing more, and that Boaz protects her honor before he protects his own interest. For an Israel that could quote Deuteronomy 23:3 against Moabites, the author is building a case, verse by verse, that a Moabite woman's loyal kindness can outstrip anything native born virtue produces, and that such faithfulness deserves marriage into the covenant people, not exclusion from it. He is also quietly answering any suspicion a later reader might carry about David's own great grandmother: this is how the line of Israel's king began, in honor, not in scandal, at a threshing floor where two people trusted God's law more than their own convenience.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Nothing in this chapter licenses a modern reader to stage a private, after dark visit to propose marriage; the specific actions belong to Israelite law and custom and are not a pattern to imitate directly. What does transfer is the shape of righteous behavior under pressure: Ruth risks her reputation for the sake of covenant loyalty rather than self interest, and Boaz, alone with a vulnerable woman at midnight, chooses her protection over his own advantage without needing a law to force him. The chapter also models a way of pursuing what is right through legitimate, existing structures, kinsman redemption and the elders at the gate, rather than around them; Boaz does not simply keep Ruth, he insists on settling the nearer kinsman's claim first. Believers today follow the same shape, not the same customs, when they choose integrity over expedience and pursue their desires through legitimate means rather than shortcuts.

debates.question: Was there anything improper in Ruth's night approach to Boaz?

views.label: A chaste, honorable appeal
views.case: The narrative underscores Ruth's virtue and Boaz's restraint; uncovering his feet and asking for his garment are covenant gestures of a marriage proposal and protection, and Boaz responds by guarding her reputation and blessing her character. Nothing immoral occurs.

views.label: A bold, risky act redeemed by integrity
views.case: The scene is charged and dangerous by design, and Ruth takes a real risk to her honor; yet both act rightly, and the very tension magnifies their integrity and God's overruling providence.

debates.bearing: Either way the text presents Ruth and Boaz as righteous, so the scene showcases faith and integrity rather than intrigue, and points to a redeemer who protects rather than exploits the vulnerable.

debates.question: What does the request to spread the garment mean?

views.label: A proposal of marriage and redemption
views.case: Spreading the corner of a garment over a woman was a recognized act of betrothal and protection; Ruth links it directly to Boaz being a kinsman-redeemer, so she is asking him to marry her and take up the redeemer's role.

views.label: An appeal for covenant covering
views.case: The gesture echoes 2:12, taking refuge under the wings of God, and Ezekiel 16:8, where God spreads His garment over His people; Ruth is asking to be brought under covenant protection.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge: Ruth asks to be covered, married, and redeemed, a request that pictures the covenant covering God gives His people in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Naomi's menuchah in verse 1 is not a new word to this book: she used it in 1:9 to bless Ruth and Orpah with rest in a husband's house, and now she moves from wishing it to engineering it. The word covers more than sleep; it names the settled security of a household where a woman is no longer exposed, exactly what a widow without land or husband lacked in ancient Israel.

The chapter's verb of choice is shakab, to lie down, which occurs repeatedly across the scene, of Boaz settling for the night, verse 7, Ruth positioning herself, verses 7 and 8, and Boaz instructing her to stay, verses 13 and 14. Repetition this dense is not accidental; the narrator wants the reader's attention fixed on the single physical posture around which the whole scene turns, without ever describing anything more than lying down at the feet.

Ruth's appeal in verse 9 layers three loaded words together. She names herself Boaz's servant, asks him to spread his kanaph, wing or garment corner, over her, and calls him a goel. The kanaph is the same word Boaz used in 2:12 for the wings of the God of Israel under which Ruth had come to take refuge; she is asking the man who blessed her under God's wings to become those wings in the flesh. Goel names a specific legal office, the near relative bound to redeem land or redeem a person from debt slavery, Leviticus 25:25-55 and Numbers 35:19, and Ruth applies it here to marriage and inheritance, a use the legal texts do not spell out in so many words but which the narrative treats as a natural extension of the redeemer's care for the family's whole future.

Boaz answers with chesed, the loyal, covenant shaped kindness that has named Ruth from her first appearance, 1:8 and 2:20, and now describes her choice of an older redeemer over a younger husband as an even greater instance of that same virtue. He then names her an eshet chayil, a woman of strength or worth, the very phrase Proverbs 31:10 uses of the ideal wife, and the mirror image of his own description as a gibbor chayil, a man of standing, in 2:1. The pairing of chayil with chayil across the two characters signals to a Hebrew ear that a match of equals is being made, worth answering worth.

Finally, the verb yada, to know or recognize, frames the chapter's concern for secrecy: Boaz warns Ruth not to let it be known, literally not to let herself be recognized, verse 14, that a woman had come to the threshing floor, guarding her reputation with the same care the narrator has shown in describing her request. The word choices throughout keep pointing past a private romance toward a public, legal, covenant act.

typology.type: Boaz spreads his garment over the exposed and vulnerable Ruth
typology.fulfillment: Boaz's answer to Ruth's request is not merely permission but action he genuinely undertakes: to spread a garment over someone in the ancient world was to claim her as family and take responsibility for her future. Ezekiel 16:8 shows the LORD doing exactly this over defenseless Jerusalem, spreading His cloak and entering covenant with her. Ephesians 5:25-27 escalates the picture further: Christ does not merely cover a bride's shame but washes and sanctifies her until she is presented without stain or wrinkle. Boaz's covering removes danger for one night; Christ's covering removes guilt forever, and unlike Boaz He cannot fail to keep His pledge.

typology.type: Ruth's humble appeal to the one who alone can redeem her
typology.fulfillment: Ruth comes to Boaz at her most exposed, with nothing to offer but her need and her claim on his kindness, and she is received rather than refused. That posture anticipates every sinner's approach to Christ, who does not ask for merit before He grants mercy, Romans 5:8. The escalation is that Ruth still had to trust a good but fallible man who might, in principle, have taken advantage of her; those who come to Christ trust a Redeemer who cannot sin against them, who welcomes the needy as freely as Boaz did and fails them in nothing, Hebrews 4:15-16.

typology.type: Boaz's vow that the redemption will not wait
typology.fulfillment: Boaz tells Ruth he will not rest until redemption is settled, and true to his word he goes to the gate the very next morning, Ruth 4:1. His urgency contrasts with every long deferred human promise and points to the Redeemer who, having set His face to accomplish redemption, pressed on without wavering until He could declare it finished, John 19:30. The type falls short in scale rather than character, since Boaz secures one family's future for a season while Christ secures His people's future forever, and no nearer claimant can ever set aside what He has already settled.

study.christ:
Boaz's whole bearing toward Ruth traces the character of the Redeemer to come by contrast and by anticipation, not by allegorizing every detail. He is not compelled to help her; he chooses to, delighting more in her latest kindness than he did in her first, a picture of a Redeemer whose love toward His people is not merely dutiful but glad. When she asks him to take her under his protection, he does not treat the request as either an imposition or an opportunity, and Scripture elsewhere links exactly this posture, refusing to take advantage of the vulnerable, to the character it expects of anyone who reflects the LORD, Psalm 15:1-5.

The pattern reaches further than one good man's integrity. Boaz insists on due process even when he wants to redeem Ruth immediately; he will not simply take what he desires but goes to the gate the next morning to secure it lawfully, in the sight of witnesses. Christ's redemption of His people likewise proceeds through righteousness rather than around it, He bore the law's full claim against sinners rather than setting it aside, Romans 3:25-26, so that God is both just and the justifier of those who trust in Jesus.

There is also a contrast worth naming honestly. Boaz cannot redeem Ruth without cost to himself, since acquiring Elimelech's land and a wife obligates him to raise up an heir who will one day divide what would otherwise be entirely his own family's inheritance, a cost the nearer kinsman was unwilling to bear, Ruth 4:6. Christ's redemption costs infinitely more, not land or inheritance but His own blood, and unlike Boaz He gains nothing for Himself by it except the joy of a people He already loved, Hebrews 12:2.

The connection to David matters here too. This scene, still two generations from David, is quietly shaping the ancestry of Israel's king, and Matthew's genealogy will run this same line to great David's greater Son, Matthew 1:5-6. A story about one widow's rescue turns out to be part of how God prepared the house from which the Messiah would come, so that the Redeemer readers meet centuries later at a Bethlehem manger has His human roots partly in a threshing floor outside that same town.
study.god:
The book of Ruth is famous for narrating providence without a single miracle: no angel appears, no voice speaks from heaven, and yet every character treats the LORD as active in what looks, on the surface, like ordinary human planning and choice. Naomi's scheme, Ruth's obedience, and Boaz's integrity are never set against God's sovereignty as though one crowds out the other; the narrator simply lets human faithfulness and divine rule occupy the same sentence without explanation, which is itself a claim about how God usually works.

This chapter in particular shows a God who cares about the vulnerable being protected rather than merely provided for. Israel's law repeatedly names widows alongside orphans and foreigners as those the LORD watches with special care, warning that He will hear their cry if they are wronged, Exodus 22:22-24, and Boaz's refusal to take advantage of Ruth at her most exposed embodies exactly the character that law was meant to produce in every Israelite with power over someone weaker. God's concern for the vulnerable is not abstract policy; it shapes what a man does alone at midnight when no one else is watching.

The chapter also deepens the theology of rest that runs through the whole Torah. The security Naomi seeks for Ruth is a small, domestic version of the same rest God gives Israel in the land, Deuteronomy 12:9-10, and the Sabbath rest built into creation itself, Genesis 2:2-3. A God who cares about one widow's household security is the same God whose entire redemptive purpose aims at rest for His people, a thread Hebrews later gathers up into the rest that remains for God's people, Hebrews 4:9-11.

Finally, the chapter shows God at work through ordinary legal and social structures rather than around them. He does not need Boaz to break custom or override the nearer kinsman's rights to accomplish His purposes; His providence moves through elders, gates, sandals, and blessings, showing a God who is patient with process and who does not need to force outcomes to secure what He has determined to do.

crossReferences.note: Naomi's plan in chapter three finally acts on the blessing she spoke over Ruth and Orpah at the very start of the book, that each would find a resting place in a husband's house. Her scheme is not new hope but old hope she now takes concrete steps to fulfill.

Boaz once prayed that Ruth would be richly repaid by the LORD, under whose wings she had taken refuge. At the threshing floor Ruth asks Boaz himself to spread that same wing over her, effectively asking the man who prayed the blessing to become the answer to his own prayer.

The LORD describes His covenant with Jerusalem in exactly Ruth's language, spreading His garment over a helpless, exposed woman and pledging Himself to her. Boaz's action at the threshing floor is a small, human echo of the LORD's own pattern of covenant love toward the needy and the shamed.

The law lays out the redeemer's duty to buy back land a poor relative has been forced to sell, establishing the legal category Ruth invokes when she calls Boaz a kinsman redeemer. Ruth 3 and 4 apply that same office to a widow and her inheritance together.

The poem asks who can find a wife of noble character and lists her worth above jewels. Boaz calls Ruth exactly this in verse 11, so that a foreign widow gleaning in a stranger's field is publicly declared to match the ideal of Israel's own wisdom literature.

The law warns Israel not to mistreat a widow, promising that the LORD Himself will hear her cry. Boaz, alone with a widow at her most vulnerable, protects rather than exploits her, embodying in one private, unwitnessed act exactly what that law demanded of every Israelite with power over the weak.

The psalm describes the one fit to dwell with the LORD as a person who keeps a costly promise and does no harm to a neighbor even when harm would cost nothing. Boaz's restraint with Ruth, and his insistence on honoring the nearer kinsman's rights, trace that same portrait of integrity.

Christ's love for the church is described in the same key of covering and cleansing that Boaz shows toward Ruth, except Paul describes a bridegroom who sanctifies and washes his bride until she is without any stain, going far beyond shelter for a night to a righteousness that lasts forever.

The rest Naomi sought for Ruth in a husband's house becomes, in this letter, the Sabbath rest that remains for the whole people of God. The small, domestic security a widow needed in Bethlehem is one thread in a much larger promise of rest that only Christ secures fully.

study.oneStory:
Every strand of this chapter reaches back to the fracture in Eden and forward to its repair. Naomi and Ruth are exposed exactly the way the fall exposes every person, without land, without an heir, without the covering a household was meant to provide, echoes of Adam and Eve's own nakedness and need for God to clothe them, Genesis 3:21. What God did directly there, He now does through an ordinary man's willingness to spread his garment over a needy woman, showing that the same compassion that clothed the first sinners still moves through faithful people in every generation.

The scene also sits inside redemption's long middle chapter, after the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his line, Genesis 12:3, and before that promise narrows to David and finally to Christ. A Moabite woman, one of the very nations under a cloud of exclusion, Deuteronomy 23:3, is welcomed at a threshing floor into the family that will bear the Messiah, a small but real preview of the nations streaming into the same redemption centuries later, Ephesians 2:12-13.

Ruth's appeal for covering and Boaz's pledge to secure it without delay anticipate the moment redemption is finally and fully settled, not at a gate in Bethlehem but at a cross outside Jerusalem, where the true Redeemer paid every claim against His people at once and declared the matter closed, John 19:30. What Ruth risked everything to ask for, covering, security, a future, sinners now receive freely in Christ, who did not wait to be asked before He set His face to redeem us.

And the chapter's small, hopeful ending, grain enough to fill an empty shawl, points toward the last chapter of the whole story, where the emptied and exiled finally sit down at a wedding feast, clothed not in six measures of barley but in fine linen, bright and pure, the righteous acts of the saints, Revelation 19:7-8, and given rest, not for one night on a threshing floor, but forever in the presence of God.

sermon.title: Ruth Proposes to Boaz
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Ruth, this message expounds Ruth 3:6-18, the threshing floor scene, Ruth's appeal for covering, and Boaz as kinsman-redeemer foreshadowing Christ, showing how the blood of Christ covers His people. A faithful, expository handling of this movement's climax.

quiz.q: Why did Naomi send Ruth to the threshing floor?

options.text: To seek a resting place, the security of marriage and a home, through Boaz the redeemer.
options.note: Ruth 3:1 states Naomi's aim to find a resting place so it would be well with Ruth.

options.text: To glean more grain during the night.
options.note: The grain comes later as a gift; the purpose of the visit was to seek redemption and rest.

options.text: To confront Boaz about unfair wages.
options.note: There is no dispute over wages; the aim was marriage and redemption.

options.text: To ask Boaz for a loan.
options.note: Naomi sought a resting place through redemption, not money.

quiz.q: What did Ruth ask of Boaz at the threshing floor?

options.text: To spread the corner of his garment over her, because he was a kinsman-redeemer.
options.note: Ruth 3:9 records her appeal for covering and redemption, in effect a marriage proposal.

options.text: To give her a permanent job among his workers.
options.note: She sought redemption and covering, which is far more than employment.

options.text: To hide her from the nearer kinsman.
options.note: She asked for his covering as redeemer; Boaz himself later raises the nearer kinsman.

options.text: To take her back to Moab.
options.note: Ruth had bound herself to Israel and its God; she sought a home there, not a return.

quiz.q: How did Boaz respond to Ruth's request?

options.text: With blessing and honor, promising to act, but noting a nearer redeemer must be given first refusal.
options.note: Ruth 3:10-13 shows his integrity: willing to redeem, yet honoring the nearer kinsman.

options.text: By rejecting her outright.
options.note: He did not reject her; he blessed her and pledged to secure her redemption.

options.text: By taking advantage of her vulnerability.
options.note: The text stresses his integrity and protection of her honor, the opposite of exploitation.

options.text: By sending her away in anger.
options.note: He responded with kindness, blessing, and a firm promise to act.

quiz.q: What does Boaz spreading his garment over Ruth picture?

options.text: Christ covering His people with His righteousness and taking them as His own.
options.note: The covering echoes God spreading His garment over His people in covenant, Ezekiel 16:8.

options.text: A mere social custom with no deeper meaning.
options.note: It is a real custom, but Scripture uses it as a picture of covenant covering.

options.text: That Ruth had done something shameful.
options.note: The covering signals protection and betrothal, not shame.

options.text: That Boaz was claiming her property unfairly.
options.note: It is an act of protection and redemption, not a property grab.

quiz.q: What did Naomi say about Boaz at the end of the chapter?

options.text: That he would not rest until he had resolved the matter that very day.
options.note: Ruth 3:18 shows Boaz's resolve, foreshadowing the Redeemer who finishes His work.

options.text: That he had likely forgotten his promise already.
options.note: Naomi was confident he would act at once, not that he would forget.

options.text: That Ruth should look for another man.
options.note: Naomi told Ruth to wait, trusting Boaz to settle it.

options.text: That the nearer kinsman would surely refuse.
options.note: Naomi did not predict the outcome; she trusted Boaz to resolve it that day.

questions: Ruth took a humble, bold step of faith, trusting Boaz to act as her redeemer. Where is God calling you to a bold step of faith, casting yourself on His mercy?
Boaz protected Ruth's honor when he could have exploited her. How does his integrity challenge the way you treat others, especially when you hold power over them?
Ruth asked to be covered by her redeemer. How does it comfort you that Christ covers your shame with His own righteousness?
Boaz would not rest until redemption was settled. How does knowing that Christ finished the work of your salvation give you rest today?
Naomi's counsel was, wait until you see how things turn out. Where do you need to trust and wait while God works out a matter you cannot control?

translationNotes.note: Resting place renders menuchah, security and a settled home; Naomi seeks for Ruth the rest that marriage and redemption would bring.

Spread the corner of your garment translates a phrase using kanaph, wing or corner of a garment; the BSB footnote notes it can be rendered spread your wing, echoing 2:12. It is a gesture of betrothal and protection.
A woman of noble character renders eshet chayil, the same phrase as Proverbs 31:10 and the counterpart to Boaz as a man of chayil in 2:1.
Six measures of barley was a generous load; the BSB footnote suggests possibly six seahs, and the gift signals Boaz's pledge that Ruth would not go home empty-handed.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ruth 3:1-18. Footnotes on verse 9 (garment or wing) and verse 15 (six measures) are reflected in the translation notes.
